sec.title: Background
sec.p: The Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II) builds on the landmark study Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study to develop real-world implementation strategies for preventing type 2 diabetes (T2DM). This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of digital and complex lifestyle intervention in reducing the incidence of T2DM among adults with increased risk of T2DM, compared to usual care over a 36-month period.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A three-arm, stratified, cluster-randomized controlled trial will be conducted in eight factories in Daqing, with clusters as the unit of randomization and individual participants as the unit of analysis. Fifty-seven clusters will be randomly allocated (1:1:1) to one of three groups: (1) Digital-based lifestyle intervention, (2) complex lifestyle intervention, or (3) usual care. Eligible participants will be adults aged 25–55 with increased risk of T2DM, defined by IFG, IGT, HbA1c 5.7–6.4%, and/or 1-h PG above 8.6 mmol/L, while not meeting the criteria for diabetes. Exclusion criteria include significant cardiovascular disease (CVD) within 6 months, impaired liver function, renal dysfunction, other significant medical or psychological conditions, or participation in similar studies. The interventions will run for 3 years. The primary outcomes are the 3-year cumulative incidence of T2DM. The study will utilize the RE-AIM framework and Implementation Outcome Framework (IOF) to assess Reach, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance, Feasibility, Acceptability, and Appropriateness through process measures. Data collection will include plasma glucose (0, 1, and 2 h) and insulin levels (0, 1, and 2 h) based on the oral glucose tolerance test, laboratory tests, blood pressure, body mass index, waist circumference, and dietary and physical activity behaviors, diabetes knowledge, and quality of life. These measures will be assessed by trained doctors or nurses at baseline and at 6-,12-, 24-, and 36-month follow-ups.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The study will provide evidence on how population-level strategies of digital and complex lifestyle intervention can be implemented in real-world settings to prevent diabetes. If proven effective, these strategies could be integrated into Workplace Wellness Program in China and other countries to prevent diabetes and other noncommunicable diseases.

sec.title: Background and rationale {6a}
sec.p: In recent decades, China has seen a rapid increase in the disease burden of diabetes [1]. Globally, China has the largest number of individuals aged 20–79 years living with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), with 140.9 million cases in 2021. This number is projected to rise to 174.4 million by 2045 [2]. T2DM also imposes a significant economic burden on China, with the total cost of diabetes reaching US $250.2 billion in 2020 and increasing at an annual rate of 6.32%, exceeding the country’s overall economic growth rate [1]. With over 100 million people in China already living with T2DM, there is an urgent need to strengthen early detection, diagnosis, and treatment. However, a national survey conducted in 2018 found that more than half (63.3%) of individuals with diabetes remain undiagnosed, only one-third (32.9%) receive treatment, and, among those treated, only half (50.1%) had adequate glycemic control [3]. In light of these challenges, immediate action is essential to prevent T2DM.

Prediabetes is characterized by impaired fasting glucose (IFG), impaired glucose tolerance (IGT), or elevated HbA1c (nondiabetic hyperglycemia — NDH) [4]. It represents an intermediate metabolic state that precedes T2DM. Although the progression rate varies across populations, on average, nearly 5–10% of individuals with prediabetes develop T2DM each year, and nearly 70% will eventually progress to T2DM unless effective intervention occurs [5]. For example, the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study in China reported that 93% of individuals with IGT in the control group developed diabetes over a 20-year follow-up period [6]. Even more concerning, 38.1% of adults aged 18 or older in China have prediabetes [3], which not only increases the risk of developing T2DM but also raises the risk of microvascular and macrovascular complications, as well as all-cause and cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality [7]. Given these risks, proactively addressing prediabetes should be a key priority in diabetes prevention efforts in China. Most diabetes prevention programs have focused on individuals with IGT, while evidence supporting the effectiveness of lifestyle interventions in individuals with isolated IFG (i-IFG) or NDH remains limited [8]. Recently, the International Diabetes Federation (IDF) defined prediabetes to include individuals with a 1-h post-load plasma glucose (1-h PG) value of 155 mg/dL (8.6 mmol/L) or higher, recommending lifestyle interventions and referral to diabetes prevention programs [9]. However, this approach requires rigorous evaluation, especially in real-world settings and resource-limited environments.

Efficacy studies from many countries have consistently demonstrated that lifestyle modification is an effective intervention to prevent or delay the onset of diabetes in individuals with prediabetes [10]. However, the benefits depend on successful implementation in real-world settings [11]. The Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study, one of the most landmark randomized control trials for diabetes prevention [12], demonstrated that group-based, face-to-face lifestyle interventions delayed diabetes onset by a median of 4 years, with beneficial effects sustained for up to three decades [13]. Despite this, no implementation study in China has adopted the Daqing model. In contrast, many studies conducted in Europe, the USA, and some Asian countries have primarily followed the US Diabetes Prevention Program (US-DPP) model [11]. Additionally, the limited effectiveness of lifestyle interventions that focus solely on diet and physical activity suggests that multifactorial lifestyle interventions should be implemented in at-risk populations [14, 15].Therefore, there is a pressing need for effective, scalable, and sustainable models to identify individuals with prediabetes and to deliver personalized, evidence-based lifestyle interventions.

Strategies are urgently needed to prevent and manage both T2DM and prediabetes. The existing implementation studies have primarily focused on face-to-face counselling, delivered either individually or in groups [11]. However, limited face-to-face time with participants poses a challenge to deliver counselling effectively in real-world settings [16]. Future research should explore models for lower-intensity face-to-face and hybrid lifestyle interventions. Although digital interventions are generally more scalable than traditional face-to-face approaches [17–19], adherence remains a significant challenge. Evidence from developed countries suggests that digital-based lifestyle interventions can support weight control; [20, 21] however, there is limited evidence regarding their effectiveness in diabetes prevention [22, 23]. For instance, a study found that a combination of digital and face-to-face group lifestyle interventions, but not digital-only interventions, improved overall diet quality in real-world settings among individuals with prediabetes [12, 24]. Therefore, the impact of digital interventions on diabetes prevention remains unclear. Furthermore, the importance of a supportive environment should not be overlooked [25]. Evidence suggests that support from family [26] and peers [27], which is typically present in group-based interventions, plays a crucial role in their effectiveness [28]. Additionally, the workplace environment plays a vital role in supporting employees’ health. For example, workplace cafeterias are key settings for providing access to healthy meals [29]. Hence, further studies are needed to develop and evaluate more feasible lifestyle intervention models for developing countries in real-world settings.

To date, no large-scale RCTs in China have followed the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study while incorporating behavioral change techniques. The Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study II (Daqing DPS-II) aims to adapt and implement the evidence-based lifestyle intervention from the original Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study in real-world settings. This paper outlines the protocol for identifying and recruiting individuals with prediabetes and conducting a randomized controlled trial to assess the effectiveness of digital and complex lifestyle intervention compared with usual care. Importantly, the risk identification and lifestyle intervention components will be fully integrated into the employees’ Wellness Program, facilitating long-term implementation.

sec.title: Objectives {7}
sec.p: This hybrid type II, three-arm, parallel cluster randomized trial aims to evaluate the effectiveness and implementation of digital and complex lifestyle intervention in preventing T2DM, as identified through a two-stage screening program.

sec.title: Primary objective
sec.p: To investigate the effectiveness and implementation of digital and complex lifestyle intervention, compared to usual care, in preventing the incidence of T2DM among individuals with prediabetes at 36-month follow-up, using a hybrid type II, three-arm, parallel cluster randomized trial.

sec.title: Secondary objectives
sec.p:
To investigate the effectiveness of digital and complex lifestyle intervention over the short term (assessed at 6 months), medium term (assessed at 12 and 24 months), and longer term (assessed at 36 months) on the following:
Behavioral outcome: Physical activity, sedentary behavior, diet, and sleep
Psychosocial outcome: Self-efficacy, depression, stress, anxiety, and health-related quality of life
Physical measurement: Blood pressure, waist circumference, hip circumference, body mass index, and bioimpedance
Biochemical measurement: FPG, 1-h PG, 2-h PG, fasting insulin, 1-h insulin, 2-h insulin, and HbA1c, lipid profile (these outcomes are not assessed at the 6-month follow-up).
Reversion to normoglycemia

sec.title: Trial design {8}
sec.p: This is a three-arm cluster randomized controlled trial comparing the effects of digital and complex lifestyle intervention with usual care, in adults with increased T2DM risk, with the goal of reducing the risk of developing diabetes over 3 years. For practical reasons and to minimize the risk of contamination from contacts within the same workplace, clusters will serve as the unit of randomization, while individual participants will serve as the unit of analysis.

The research design also includes an evaluation of healthcare cost. The study will apply the RE-AIM framework and the Implementation Outcome Framework (IOF) to assess key dimensions such as Reach, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance, Feasibility, Acceptability, and Appropriateness. These implementation outcomes will be measured using a mixed-methods approach through a set of predefined process measures.

sec.title: Study setting {9}
sec.p: The study is being conducted in Daqing city, located in Heilongjiang province in the northeastern part of China. Daqing is named after Daqing Oilfield, China’s largest and world’s fourth most productive oilfield. The health and wellness of employees in the oilfield have been prioritized as part of the plan to implement Healthy China 2030. As a result, Daqing provides an ideal setting to implement and evaluate a lifestyle modification program. We are currently recruiting employees in eight factories in Daqing.

sec.title: Eligibility criteria {10}
sec.p:
The inclusion criteria are as follows:
Participants aged 25–55 years
Prediabetes defined as IFG (FPG 5.6–6.9 mmol/L), IGT (2-h PG 7.8–11.0 mmol/L during oral glucose tolerance test [OGTT]), or elevated HbA1c (5.7%–6.4% [39–47 mmol/L]) or 1-h PG ≥ 8.6 mmol/L, while not being defined as diabetes
Employees in the Daqing Oilfield
Possibility to use a computer, smartphone, or tablet with Internet connection
Willingness to sign the written informed consent form

The exclusion criteria are as follows:
Significant CVD within 6 months (acute myocardial infarction, class III/IV congestive heart failure defined by the New York Heart Association (NYHA), left ventricular ejection fraction ≤ 40% or cerebrovascular accident)
Impaired liver function (including obvious clinical signs or symptoms of liver disease, acute or chronic hepatitis, ALT or AST levels ≥ 3 times the upper limit of the reference range at the screening visit)
Renal dysfunction (eGFR < 45 mL/min)
Participation in projects involving lifestyle modifications or other clinical trials within 30 days
Any other significant medical or psychological condition that could endanger the health of the participant or confound the study results if the participant is enrolled

sec.title: Who will take informed consent? {26a}
sec.p: Informed consent is obtained by trained doctors or nurses from the clinic, known as the “Diabetes Prevention Working Group,” designated by the Daqing Oilfield General Hospital for the Daqing DPS-II study (hereafter referred to as the local implementation team). Written consent is provided by the participants. The informed consent form is included in the Additional File 1. While written consent from the clusters will not be obtained, the clusters agree to participate and cooperate with the study team to facilitate follow-up data collection and intervention design and delivery.

sec.title: Additional consent provisions for collection and use of participant data and biological specimens {26b}
sec.p: Consent includes the option for participants to grant permission for the collection and use of participant data and biological specimens.

sec.title: Theory of intervention
sec.p:
The intervention will address barriers and facilitators to adopt a healthy lifestyle, as identified based on the COM-B model [30], and will incorporate the relevant behavioral change techniques [31, 32], including goal-setting, problem-solving, action planning, reviewing behavior goals, feedback, self-monitoring, instruction on how to perform behavior, information about health consequences, and social support. The intervention will be delivered not only through face-to-face group-based meetings but also via personalized approaches, including web-based apps specifically designed for the trial, motivational interviews conducted by telephone or WeChat, and in-person consultations. Additionally, social support, including peer support and family support, will be promoted to help participants make lifestyle changes. Implementation strategies will be developed to promote the delivery of the intervention. The program objectives will be achieved through a combination of individual learning and environmental change, using evidence-based behavioral change techniques and strategies that address behavioral determinants at different levels (Fig. 1).Fig. 1
Program goals, theory-based methods, and strategies. To achieve the goal, modification of these lifestyle components is necessary: physical activity, healthy eating, stress management, tobacco cessation, and alcohol limitation. Each component has specific behavioral targets. Each component incorporates behavioral change techniques at different levels

sec.title: Intervention content
sec.p: Figure 2 shows a thematic representation of program goals, targets, and strategies adopted at different levels. The intervention will primarily focus on key behavioral risk factors, including unhealthy eating, insufficient physical activity, and weight management. Based on the dietary recommendation for the prevention of T2DM and relevant research findings among individuals with prediabetes, the dietary intervention will promote a balanced, low-calorie diet (1800–2000 kcal per day), which is 500 kcal lower than the daily requirement for adults who are not overweight or obese and 500–700 kcal lower for those with overweight or obesity. Other dietary recommendations include increasing the intake of whole grains, fruits and vegetables, milk, and water, replacing red meat with white meat, choosing low-energy and low-GI food, reducing the consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages and processed food (especially highly processed items), and dining out or ordering takeout.

The dietary goals include the following:
500 g of vegetables intake per day
200–350 g of fruit intake per day
Eight cups (1500–1700 mL) of water per day
Limit intake of sugar-sweetened beverage

Additional lifestyle goals include the following:
Engage in physical activity for at least 150 min of moderate or vigorous aerobic activity per week
Participate in resistance activities every other day, for at least twice a week, and 7–8 h of sleep at night
Do not smoke
Avoid use of alcohol

Weight management goals include the following:
For individuals who are overweight or obese, achieve 5–10% weight loss
For individuals at a healthy weight, maintain current weight

The core interventions are structured across multiple levels. The mediating factors are hypothesized to represent the pathways of change linked to each component of the core interventions. Each mediating factor is designed to illustrate how a specific component leads to change, while the corresponding indicators quantify the extent of that change. sec.title: Usual care arm
sec.p: Participants in the usual care arm will receive electronic educational materials via the official WeChat webpage of the Daqing DPS-II Study. Information on risk factors for T2DM, along with the recommendations for healthy eating, physical activity, sleep, and lifestyle modification skills, will be updated every Tuesday. One face-to-face group session will be held during the collection of additional baseline data, during which participants will be introduced to the trial and informed about the potential benefits from participation. During this session, participants will also receive personalized feedback on their behavioral assessment, blood pressure, anthropometric measurements, and biochemical data collected at the time of OGTT. The study team’s contact information will be provided to the participants for any study-related inquiries. Participants can ask questions about weight and glucose control in the WeChat group, and an endocrinologist from the local implementation team will monitor the WeChat group and respond to participant queries within 12 h.

sec.title: Digital-based lifestyle intervention arm
sec.p: In addition to the activities provided in the usual care arm, participants in the digital-based lifestyle intervention group will receive a personalized, habit-based intervention for a period of 36 months. The digital intervention, which focused on diet, physical activity, and weight management planning and action, is delivered via a web-based application, specifically designed for this study. The application was developed through a collaborative process involving researchers from the fields of behavioral science, nutrition, physical activity, psychology, and medicine, along with a local implementation team and participants’ representatives. It is compatible with smart devices, such as computers, tablets, and smart phones, and does not require installing a separate application. Participants are instructed to use the application in the maintenance stage (7 months–36 months). During the first-time use, the participant will log in with personal information. Usage of the application will be monitored through log data collected throughout the intervention. Additionally, participants will receive 16 motivational counselling sessions delivered via telephone or WeChat messages by trained doctors or nurses from the local implementation team to support participants with their behavioral change efforts. These contacts will be made monthly during the first 6 months and then once every quarter for the remainder of the intervention.

sec.title: Complex lifestyle intervention arm
sec.p: During the group sessions, participants will discuss and share their behaviors, set SMART (Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, and Time-bound) goals, and regularly monitor and review their progress. The sessions will cover a range of topics, including diet, physical activity, sleep, stress management, tobacco cessation, and reduction of alcohol use (Fig. 3).

Trained doctors or nurses from the Diabetes Prevention Working Group will measure the health status of participants, i.e., weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, and glucose level after each group session. Based on these measurements, trained doctors or nurses will provide face-to-face, individual-based lifestyle modification and weight management consultation for participants accordingly.

Family members of the participants are encouraged to support lifestyle modification by their loved ones. A letter from the study will be sent to the participants’ families, emphasizing the important role they can play in encouraging and helping participants develop action plans for lifestyle change.

The study will call for potential peer leaders who are willing to be contacted for research purposes and share their stories with other participants regarding healthy eating, physical activity, and weight management. These peer leaders will be identified to encourage participants to attend the group-based meetings and motivate them to change their behaviors, with ongoing instructional support from the local implementation team. The Health, Safety, and Environment (HSE) liaisons in the workplace will also be invited to provide support for participants.

sec.title: Criteria for discontinuing or modifying allocated interventions {11b}
sec.p: If participants progress to diabetes based on self-monitoring glucose test, they will be invited to undergo an OGTT at the “Diabetes Prevention Working Group” clinic. If FPG ≥ 7.0 mmol/L or 2-h PG ≥ 11.1 mmol/L, they will be diagnosed with diabetes and referred to hospital for treatment.

sec.title: Strategies to improve adherence to interventions {11c}
sec.p: The HSE liaisons in the workplace will assist in coordinating with participants’ involvement in intervention activities. To minimize crossover contamination, the local implementation team will coordinate with HSE liaisons in each cluster to schedule group-based meetings. HSE liaisons will receive pre-defined messages and send reminders only to participants on the predefined list, to minimize inadvertent sharing of intervention information across clusters. At the end of the group-based meetings, participants will complete a short questionnaire to document their learning. To help identify any cross-arm attendance, the questionnaire will collect the participant’s initials and last six digits of their ID.

At the 6-month and 12-month follow-up data collection, participants will also have their cardiovascular disease risk assessed using the artificial intelligence retinal expert, with the aim to increase their adherence to intervention. All participants will sign an attendance sheet during each group session.

sec.title: Relevant concomitant care permitted or prohibited during the trial {11d}
sec.p: Participants will continue to receive usual care throughout the trial, with no restrictions on their standard medical care or lifestyle choices.

sec.title: Provisions for posttrial care {30}
sec.p: Usual care is provided through the Wellness Program at the Daqing Oilfield workplace.

sec.title: Primary outcome
sec.p: The primary outcome measure is the incidence of T2DM based on the 2023 ADA criteria: FPG ≥ 7.0 mmol/L, 2-h PG ≥ 11.1 mmol/L, or HbA1c > 6.5% or diagnosed by physicians.

sec.title: Secondary outcome
sec.p:
Secondary outcome measures include the following:
Behaviors: Physical activity, diet, sleep, and weight management
Psychosocial factors: Depression, stress, anxiety, health-related quality of life and social support, weight management intention, and self-efficacy for healthy eating and physical activity
Physical measurement: Blood pressure, waist circumference, hip circumference, body mass index, and bioimpedance
Biochemical measurements are as follows:
▪ Glycemic control: Fasting plasma glucose, 1-h post-glucose load, 2-h post-glucose load, fasting insulin, 1-h post-insulin, 2-h post-insulin, and HbA1c
▪ Reversion to normoglycemia: All three measures of FPG, 2-h OGTT glucose, and HbA1c below normoglycemic thresholds (FPG < 5.6 mmol/L, 2-h PG < 7.8 mmol/L, HbA1c < 5.7%) are defined as reversion to normoglycemia.
▪ Others: Lipid profile, serum uric acid, and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR)

sec.title: Sample size {14}
sec.p: Assuming a 3-year cumulative incidence of T2DM of 29% [53] in the control group, an intra-cluster correlation of 0.05 [54], and a dropout rate of 20%, we calculated that 475 individuals in each arm would be needed to detect a 40% risk reduction [54, 55] in the intervention arm. The calculation was based on a significant level of 2.5% and type II error of 20% (i.e., power = 80%), allowing for 20% incomplete follow-up. To ensure feasibility and account for clustering effects, 19 clusters per arm, with approximately 25 participants per cluster, were included in the study design. The target sample size is 1425 participants across 57 clusters to assess the effectiveness of the digital-based lifestyle intervention and complex lifestyle intervention in reducing the incidence of T2DM over 3 years.

sec.title: Recruitment {15}
sec.p:
Eligible participants are identified by a two-stage screening process, where individuals at risk of T2DM are initially identified, and then further screened using OGTT. Approximately, 1500 participants with screen-detected prediabetes will be invited to participate in the trial (Fig. 5).Fig. 5
CONSORT flow chart. First, we identified individuals with high risk of T2DM from the 2023 health checkup database, based on venous fasting plasma glucose (FPG) between 5.6 and 7.0 mmol/L and the age between 25 and 55 years old. sec.title: Initial risk assessment
sec.p:
The participants were recruited from employees with health checkup data available for the year 2023. Eight factories with 4000 or more employees agreed to participate in the study, resulting in 7647 employees aged 25–55 being identified as at increased risk, based on venous fasting plasma glucose (FPG) ≥ 5.6 and < 7.0mmol/L. Additionally, 231 employees aged 25–55 who did not have health checkup data for 2023 were recruited based on meeting any of the following criteria:
Overweight or obese (BMI ≥ 24 kg/m2)
Family history of T2DM
Fasting capillary blood glucose of 5.6 to 6.9 mmol/L
With a random capillary blood glucose of 7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L

Individuals identified as at increased risk were invited to visit the Digital Risk Assessment Tool developed for the Daqing DPS-II. The tool includes questions adapted from the FINDRISC [56], covering factors such as age, gender, body height, body weight, waist circumference, daily physical activity, daily consumption of fruits and vegetables, smoking and alcohol use, a history of regular use of blood pressure medication, and a family history of diabetes. The tool also includes information regarding the exclusion criteria. A total of 1106 individuals were identified as meeting the exclusion criteria and were not eligible for participation.

sec.title: Examination visit for screening
sec.p: A total of 6541 individuals were identified as eligible for screening through the Digital Risk Assessment Tool and were automatically invited to visit the “Diabetes Prevention Working Group” clinic, designated by the Daqing Oilfield General Hospital for the Daqing DPS-II study. During the examination visit, participants provided informed consent and were given a flowchart outlining the data collection. They underwent a 2-h OGTT, body composition, anthropometric, and blood pressure measurements, participated in interviews to complete the questionnaires. Trained nurses collected fasting blood samples for routine laboratory tests, as well as 1-h and 2-h blood samples during the 2-h OGTTs. These samples were analyzed at the accredited clinical laboratories of the Daqing Oilfield General Hospital.

We anticipate that approximately 30% of eligible employees at each factor, yielding an estimated total of 1500 participants with screen-detected prediabetes. Recruitment numbers will be monitored weekly and strategies adjusted as needed to achieve the target sample size. These strategies include contacting HSE liaisons, reminders via WeChat or phone call, small incentives, and offering flexible appointment times. To further enhance recruitment, we extend the recruitment period, organize on-site health promotion events, and engage peer champions to encourage participation.

Out of the 2367 individuals who completed the screening, approximately 1500 were detected with prediabetes defined by the presence of IFG, IGT, HbA1c 5.7–6.4%, and/or 1-h PG above 8.6mmol/L, while not being classified as diabetes. These individuals will be invited to participate in the trial. A follow-up phone call will be arranged to invite them to join the “Group of participants” at WeChat. Afterward, they will be contacted by the HSE liaison for a face-to-face meeting, where their eligibility is confirmed; informed consent will be obtained, and additional baseline data will be collected.

sec.title: Sequence generation {16a}
sec.p: The trial employs stratified cluster randomization with zuoyequ as clusters and individual participants as the unit of analysis. The randomization process will be stratified by factory and type of work. A total of 57 clusters will be randomly allocated in a 1:1:1 ratio to one of three groups: (1) digital-based lifestyle intervention, (2) complex lifestyle intervention, or (3) usual care. Each group will receive the corresponding intervention to evaluate the effectiveness on diabetes prevention. An independent statistician, not involved in participant recruitment, data collection, or intervention delivery, will generate the randomization schedule using a computer-based sequence with variable block sizes.

sec.title: Concealment mechanism {16b}
sec.p: To ensure further concealment, randomization and allocation will be managed through a centralized, secure, password-protected system. To ensure unbiased allocation, the random assignment will be concealed from the local implementation team until the baseline survey is completed, preventing any influence on the enrolment and assessment process.

sec.title: Implementation {16c}
sec.p: The randomization will be conducted by an independent statistician. Once a cluster is confirmed eligible, the study coordinator will facilitate the local implementation team to enroll participants within the cluster. Allocation to the intervention arm will then be executed via the centralized system by an independent data manager, who will not be involved in recruitment, assessment, or analysis. The local implementation team will then enroll eligible participants into the respective clusters based on the generated allocation sequence, maintaining the integrity of the trial’s blinding and randomization.

sec.title: Who will be blinded {17a}
sec.p: Given the nature of the interventions, blinding of participants, HSE liaisons in the workplace, or the implementation team to the allocated trial arm is not feasible. However, outcome assessors will not know which intervention arm participants belong to while collecting data. The data will use ID numbers without showing intervention arm information. The statistician will also remain unaware of intervention arms until the analysis plan and code are finished and checked.

sec.title: Procedure for unblinding if needed {17b}
sec.p: Given the lifestyle nature of the interventions and their minimal risk profile, emergency unblinding is expected to be rare.

sec.title: Plans for assessment and collection of outcomes {18a}
sec.p: Data are collected at baseline and at 6, 12, 24, and 36 months. A schedule of assessments is shown in Table 2 and Fig. 4.

sec.title: Plans to promote participant retention and complete follow-up {18b}
sec.p: The implementation team will work closely with the HSE liaisons in the workplace to encourage participants to attend their follow-up appointments. Each follow-up visit will have an allowable window of 1 month before or after the scheduled visit date to accommodate participants’ availability. Whenever possible, the study follow-up visits will be aligned with the participants’ annual health checkup as a part of their Wellness Program package. This approach helps to optimize participants’ retention and adherence to the study protocol.

sec.title: Data management {19}
sec.p: Data are collected using both paper-based questionnaires and a web-based electronic questionnaire system developed for this study. All biomedical test results will be obtained from an accredited lab, and anthropometric measurements will be conducted under standardized quality control measures. All data are entered into a secure web-based platform by trained doctors or nurses from the local implementation team. To ensure privacy and confidentiality, the data are securely stored and managed by the research team, with access restricted to authorized personnel. An audit trail with timestamps and participant IDs is maintained to track any data modifications.

For paper-based questionnaires, a double data entry process is conducted by two independent staff members in the local implementation team. Any discrepancies between the two entries are automatically flagged and resolved by a third person. For web-based questionnaires, real-time logic and range checks are embedded into the system to minimize data entry errors at the point of capture. The system also allows for skip patterns and requires field checks to ensure data completeness and consistency. Range checks will be implemented in the web-based platform to prevent the entry of implausible values. Duplicate records will be automatically detected by the system and further reviewed by the local team.

The central team regularly monitors the data entry process to ensure accuracy and completeness and promptly addresses any issues related to missing or inconsistent data in coordination with the local implementation team. The database is backed up regularly using encrypted protocols to prevent data loss and to maintain data security.

sec.title: Confidentiality {27}
sec.p: Data will be stored for research purposes only, without disclosing personal identifiers. All electronic data will be stored in encrypted computers, with access restricted to authorized study team members. Publication and reports will ensure that no individual participant can be identified.
Data are not released without permission of principal investigator (PI, R. S.) to safeguard the confidentiality of the information provided by participants.

sec.title: Plans for collection, laboratory evaluation, and storage of biological specimens for genetic or molecular analysis in this trial/future use {33}
sec.p: Remaining blood samples are retained for unspecified research. These samples were processed by centrifugation within 60 min of collection to preserve their integrity. After processing, they are frozen and transported to the laboratory of the Daqing DPS-II at the CAMS/PUMC for further analysis. The biospecimen is stored in the laboratory of the Daqing DPS-II at the CAMS/PUMC in accordance with the Institutional Laboratory Management Regulations. The use is limited to research projects with a clearly defined plan approved by the principal investigator.

sec.title: Statistical methods for primary and secondary outcomes {20a}
sec.p: All analyses will follow an intention-to-treat approach, meaning that individuals will be analyzed in the group to which they were originally assigned, regardless of their adherence to the intervention. The primary objective is to evaluate the effects of the digital-based lifestyle intervention, complex lifestyle intervention, on the prevention of T2DM, relative to a usual care arm, without directly comparing the two interventions to each other. Survival curves will be used to estimate the cumulative incidence of diabetes, with the difference in incidence of T2DM tested using a two-sided log-rank test as descriptive curves. The primary time-to-event analysis of incident diabetes will use a marginal Cox proportional hazards model to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) for each intervention arm versus the usual care arm. The link/scale is log hazard. Cluster-robust (sandwich) variance will account for the cluster randomized design. The time origin will be the date of randomization. The model will adjust for a pre-specified minimal adjustment set, including intervention arm, age, gender, glycemic status, and weight status. Stratification by factory or type of work will be applied if baseline hazards differ meaningfully across factories.

The proportional hazards assumption will be assessed using scaled Schoenfeld residuals, global and covariate-specific tests, and graphical inspection of Schoenfeld residuals and log–log survival curves. If violations are detected, time-varying coefficients or stratified Cox model will be considered for the affected covariates, and alternative flexible parametric model may be explored if needed. Competing risk of death will be explored using Fine-Gray models. Since two primary comparisons will be made for primary outcome (each intervention arm vs. usual care), a Bonferroni correction will be applied to control for multiplicity, and p-values < 0.025 will be considered statistically significant. Secondary outcome will be analyzed using either generalized estimation equations (GEEs) or generalized linear mixed model (GLLM) as appropriate. Changes in secondary outcomes, including fasting glucose, 2-h glucose, weight, and waist circumference, will be analyzed across planned visits at 12, 24, and 36 months using general linear models that account for intraindividual correlations. This approach allows participants with incomplete follow-up data to contribute to the analysis and avoids reliance on comparisons at a single pre-specified time point.

sec.title: Interim analyses {21b}
sec.p: There will be no interim analyses.

sec.title: Methods for additional analyses (e.g., subgroup analyses) {20b}
sec.p: A per-protocol analysis set will be specified a priori, consisting of participants who satisfy the predefined adherence requirements, i.e., attendance at the initial intervention activity as in a previous study [57]. This set will be used for sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of the primary findings. We will explore whether the effects of the interventions on outcomes differ according to pre-specified variables, including prediabetes phenotype, baseline weight status, and gender. Subgroup differences will be formally assessed using interaction terms in the marginal Cox proportional hazards model, rather than relying on within-group p-values.
The health economic evaluation will use both a cost-effectiveness approach, assessing health gains in terms of diabetes prevented, and a cost-utility approach, assessing gains in QALYs.

A mixed- method approach will be used to evaluate implementation outcomes. Quantitative data (e.g., session attendance, learning from the group session, motivational counselling complete rates) will be collected by the local implementation team and summarized using descriptive statistics. Qualitative data will be collected by researchers from the Central Research Team at the CAMS/PUMC via structured interview, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed thematically using an inductive-deductive approach, guided by the RE-AIM and IOF frameworks. Coding and categorization will be conducted iteratively, with at least two independent researchers performing initial coding to ensure interrater reliability. Discrepancies will be resolved through discussion and consensus. A convergent mix-methods design will be employed to explore the relationship between implementation and effectiveness. Triangulation matrices will be used to integrate quantitative and qualitative findings, identifying key barriers and facilitators to intervention adoption and implementation. For qualitative data of program evaluation, the interviews will be transcribed and double-coded in NVivo 11.0 [58].

sec.title: Methods in analysis to handle protocol nonadherence and any statistical methods to handle missing data {20c}
sec.p: During the trial, we will monitor and manage missing data, aiming to keep the overall proportion of missingness below 20%. If the proportion of missing data is less than 5%, complete case analysis will be performed, as bias is expected to be minimal. For missingness between 5 and 20%, cluster-aware multiple imputation will be applied under the assumption that data are missing at random (MAR), with cluster indicators included in the imputation model to account for intra-cluster correlation. All variables used in the primary analysis, including intervention assignment, baseline covariates (e.g., age, gender, baseline glucose level), and outcome, will be included. Twenty imputed datasets will be generated, with convergence checks to ensure stable imputation, and results will be combined using Rubin’s rules. Sensitivity analysis will be conducted to check the robustness of the findings and include the following: (1) Complete-case analysis; (2) analysis exploring departures from MAR using delta-adjusted and tipping-point approaches, in which imputed values are systematically adjusted to evaluate how violations of the MAR assumption could affect the intervention effect and identify tipping points where conclusions would change; and (3) per-protocol analysis with pre-specified criteria.

sec.title: Plans to give access to the full protocol, participant-level data, and statistical code {31c}
sec.p: This document is the full protocol. Anyone interested in the aggregated version of the data may contact the corresponding author and PI (R. S.), Professor Shao (shaoruitai@cams.cn). Due to confidentiality and privacy, no identifiable participant-level data will be shared.

sec.title: Composition of the coordinating center and trial steering committee {5d}
sec.p: The “Diabetes Prevention Working Group” clinic, designated by the Daqing Oilfield General Hospital for the Daqing DPS-II study, is staffed with a team of four project managers or study coordinators, 35 doctors or nurses, and 10 laboratory technicians. The local implementation team holds weekly meetings to ensure the smooth operation of the study. On a monthly basis during the first 6 months, the project management team in the clinic is joined by the HSE liaisons in the workplace. After the first 6 months, the meetings are held on a quarterly basis for the reminder of the intervention. The central team and study steering committee oversee the project. The central team meets every 2 weeks with the local implementation team to ensure smooth operation and address any issues. The study steering committee meets every 1 or 2 months.

sec.title: Composition of the data monitoring committee and its role and reporting structure {21a}
sec.p: The Data Monitoring Committee meets on an as-needed basis. It includes an independent chair and independent members with clinical and methodological expertise, and it reports to the chair of the study steering committee. A short DMC charter summary is provided in the Additional File 3.

sec.title: Adverse event reporting and harms {22}
sec.p: Given the nature of the intervention, we do not expect serious adverse events occurring. However, we will record any adverse events including physical activity-related events (e.g., injuries, falls), disordered eating (e.g., restrictive eating behaviors, taking vomiting medication for weight loss), metabolic risks (e.g., hypoglycemia, blood glucose fluctuations), psychological distress (e.g., anxiety or guilt related to behavior change), and increased fatigue. All adverse events that meet the criteria for recording will be documented from the time a participant consents to join the trial until the end of the trial. Information about the adverse events related to study assessment is provided at the “Diabetes Prevention Working Group” clinic. The trained doctors or nurses in the local implementation team ask about the occurrence of adverse events at the time of delivery intervention or outcome assessment. The local implementation team records all relevant information on an adverse events form. The completed forms will be collected and shared with the central research team, which will submit to the Data Monitoring Committee for their review and oversight.

While participants are not prohibited from accessing intervention outside the study, concomitant care, e.g., weight-loss pharmacotherapy, outside counselling will be collected by questionnaire at follow-up visits. These data will be considered in the analysis, either as covariates in the model or in sensitivity analysis, to account for potential effects of outside interventions on study outcomes.

sec.title: Compensation for trial-related harm {30}
sec.p: Insurance or indemnity arrangements for research-related injury will be described in the informed consent form. In accordance with Chinese workplace policies, participants who are employees and take part in job-related activities will be covered by local government for occupational injury if the injury meets the statutory criteria.

sec.title: Frequency and plans for auditing trial conduct {23}
sec.p: Internal quality assurance procedures are in place to ensure regular monitoring of intervention delivery and data collection, supporting data quality and adherence to the study protocol. The central team continuously monitors various aspects of the implementation to ensure progress and compliance with protocol requirements. In addition, the trial undergoes regular monitoring and auditing by the sponsor to maintain quality control and ensure compliance with ethical and regulatory standards.

sec.title: Plans for communicating important protocol amendments to relevant parties (e.g., trial participants and ethical committees) {25}
sec.p: Any changes to the protocol require approval from both the study steering committee and the ethical committee. If amendments are necessary, all changes will be documented in a protocol change log maintained by the Central Research Team at CAMS/PUMC and communicated promptly to the local implementation team, Institutional Review Board. All approved amendments will also be updated in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry accordingly.

sec.title: Dissemination plans {31a}
sec.p: A publication and dissemination plan will be developed to ensure the findings of the trial are effectively communicated to all relevant stakeholders. The plan will include presentations at academic conferences, as well as journal publications to share the results with the wider scientific community. In addition to academic dissemination, the results will be shared with the HSE liaisons and leaders in the workplace, participants, and their families.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This cluster randomized controlled trial is the first large-scale trial conducted in a real-world setting to assess the effectiveness of digital-based lifestyle intervention and complex intervention in reducing incidence of T2DM and promoting the reversal to normoglycemia. Building on the foundation established by the Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study, the trial aims to provide valuable insights into how the Daqing model can be integrated and scaled effectively. The successful implementation of this trial will contribute to the development of a sustainable and replicable model to identify at-risk individuals and deliver evidence-based lifestyle interventions. The findings from this study have the potential to inform public health strategies not only in China but also in other countries, enhancing global efforts to prevent diabetes and improve health outcomes.

Prediabetes is a significant global public health concern, with its prevalence increasing, particularly among older adults and obese individuals [59]. Rising rates of obesity and prediabetes globally are increasing the burden of diabetes and other noncommunicable diseases. Early intervention is key, as evidence suggests that diabetes prevention strategies are most effective when implemented during the early stages of the disease [60]. However, the identification of prediabetes is complicated by the use of multiple definitions, each based on different thresholds for HbA1c, fasting glucose, and 2-h glucose levels [61]. Recently, 1-h post-load glucose has been proposed as a valuable metric for identifying prediabetes [9], though it has not yet been widely adopted in practice. The risk of progressing to diabetes varies depending on the definition of prediabetes used [59], and meeting one, two, or all glycemic criteria influences the degree of risk for developing diabetes [61]. As a result, there is a growing call for more precise risk stratification to target individuals at high or very high risk of diabetes. However, implementing evidence-based approaches to identify and intervene with individuals at increased risk of T2DM in real-world settings remains a challenge, underscoring the need for scalable and effective strategies.

The importance of early intervention in adults with prediabetes is strongly supported by findings from diabetes prevention trials [12, 62, 63]. Current guidelines recommend lifestyle modification as the primary approach for preventing diabetes in individuals with prediabetes in clinical practice, regardless of the specific definition used [4]. However, the risk of progression to diabetes varies based on how prediabetes is defined. IFG and IGT are associated with similar risks, with the highest risk observed in individuals meeting both criteria, while those identified using HbA1c thresholds have the greatest likelihood of progressing to diabetes [64]. Most major diabetes prevention trials have focused on individuals with IGT; however, the effectiveness of lifestyle interventions for those meeting IFG or HbA1c-based criteria remains less established [64]. A recent pooled analysis of 2794 participants from 4 trials in Japan, India, and the UK [65] found that lifestyle modification reduced diabetes incidence in isolated IGT (HR = 0.65, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.96) and combined IFG + IGT (HR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.68), but had no significant effect on those with isolated IFG (HR = 0.97, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.44). Furthermore, studies suggest that lifestyle intervention can promote reversion to normoglycemia, though their effectiveness depends on how prediabetes is defined [64]. A meta-analysis of 47 studies, including 26,460 participants with a mean age of 53 years, found that at a median follow-up of 1.6 years, lifestyle interventions significantly increased the likelihood of normoglycemia [66], but studies relying solely on OGTT to assess prediabetes reversion did not find significant effects. Additionally, most diabetes prevention trials have primarily focused on individuals with IFG and/or IGT, while few studies have specifically examined the effects of lifestyle modification in those with isolated IFG (i-IFG). The existing evidence suggests that lifestyle interventions are more effective for individuals whose prediabetes is characterized by glucose intolerance (IGT or combined IFG + IGT) rather than those with isolated IFG. Given that individuals identified as IFG alone tend to have a lower risk of progressing to diabetes compared to other prediabetes phenotypes, further cost-effectiveness studies are necessary to inform targeted intervention strategies based on phenotypes of prediabetes.

Despite strong evidence supporting the cost-effectiveness of lifestyle interventions in preventing diabetes and improving cardiovascular risk factors in adults with prediabetes, traditional face-to-face and group-based interventions used in landmark trials are time-consuming, expensive, and have a limited reach. Implementing these interventions in real-world practice remains challenging. The rapid advancement of mobile technologies, including apps, short message service (SMS), smartphones, or other wearable devices, offers new opportunities for public health interventions [67, 68]. Meta-analyses have demonstrated the effectiveness of digital health interventions in promoting weight loss and improving blood sugar control in individuals with prediabetes [69–71]. However, evidence on their impact on diabetes prevention and prediabetes reversion remains mixed. Some randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have shown a significant effect [72, 73], while others have found no effect [74, 75]. Additional studies are needed to evaluate the effect of digital-based interventions in diabetes prevention and prediabetes reversion. Given that individuals with prediabetes are often overweight or obese, the DPP and other trials have demonstrated that even modest weight loss can significantly reduce the risk of developing diabetes. However, weight regain remains a common challenge, potentially undermining the effectiveness of T2DM prevention efforts, even after initial success with lifestyle modifications [76]. Sustaining weight loss and achieving lasting improvements in diet and lifestyle are essential for maintaining health benefits over time. Therefore, developing acceptable, scalable, and cost-effective behavioral interventions that can be implemented in real-world settings is crucial for long-term diabetes prevention and improving public health outcomes.

One of the key strengths of our study is its real-world approach to identify individuals with elevated fasting glucose in the general population using an inexpensive and feasible annual health checkup database available through the Wellness Program in the workplace and further confirmation of prediabetes using a comprehensive assessment of hyperglycemic markers including HbA1c, FPG, 1-h PG, and 2-hPG, based on the more inclusive combined definition of the ADA guideline as well as the criteria of 1-h PG ≥ 8.6 mmol/L. By employing this inclusive screening approach, we are able to recruit individuals across all phenotypes of prediabetes and those with elevated fasting glucose, 2-h glucose, HbA1c, or 1-h glucose within the prediabetic range, as well as individuals with glycemic values at the lower end of the prediabetes spectrum. This design enables us to assess the effectiveness of lifestyle intervention in reducing diabetes risk and promoting prediabetes reversal while examining whether the benefits of such intervention vary by phenotype of prediabetes. Furthermore, our study includes a large sample of individuals representing both high- and low- risk prediabetes phenotypes, ensuring sufficient statistical power to detect the effectiveness of lifestyle intervention across different subgroups. Notably, approximately 70–80% of individuals identified with prediabetes are overweight or obese, as assessed by BMI, waist circumference, body fat percentage, and visceral fat. Additionally, about 30–40% of participants present with comorbid conditions, such as hypertension and hyperlipidemia. The 3-year duration of intervention allows for an in-depth evaluation of the long-term effects of weight change and comorbid conditions on diabetes risk and prediabetes reversion. Given the urgent need for effective and scalable lifestyle intervention for prediabetes in real-world settings, our study builds on the COM-B model to select behavior change techniques to develop interventions aiming at lifestyle modification [34]. By adopting a participatory approach, we actively engage participants, local stakeholders, and the implementation team in designing and delivering multicomponent behavioral interventions. This strategy facilitates collaboration among participants, family members, peers, and employers to address behavioral and environmental determinants of lifestyle modification based on the COM-B model. Such a structured planning process ensures a targeted approach to identify the necessary changes for effective lifestyle modification, address specific barriers and enablers, and link them to appropriate behavior change techniques. Additionally, our study employs a mixed-methods approach to evaluate not only the effectiveness of the intervention but also its implementation outcomes. This comprehensive evaluation allows for a thorough understanding of the implementation process, stakeholders’ perspectives, participants’ experiences, and the overall impact and sustainability of the interventions, contributing to the development and dissemination of scalable, evidence-based lifestyle intervention for diabetes prevention in real-world settings.

As with all trials conducted in real-world settings, there are certain limitations that must be considered when interpreting the findings of our study. First of all, this trial employs an open-label study design, meaning that both participants and investigators will be aware of the intervention assignments. However, all participants will receive some form of intervention, and allocation concealment will be ensured prior to randomization. Additionally, key personnel, like data collectors, laboratory personnel, outcome assessors, and statistician/analyst, will remain blinded to minimize potential bias. Given these precautions, the risk of bias is expected to be low. Second, the intensity of lifestyle intervention may be affected by the availability of resources, which could impact its overall effectiveness. Furthermore, participation engagement and retention may pose challenges, potentially limiting the intervention’s impact. To address this, our study incorporates a co-design approach, ensuring that the intervention is tailored to be more appealing, convenient, and accessible for participants. This strategy is expected to enhance participation and retention while also supporting the development of a cost-effective and scalable model for population-level implementation in real-world settings. Finally, as all participants in this trial are Chinese, the generalizability of the findings to other populations may be limited. However, given the growing burden of diabetes and prediabetes in Chinese and other Asian populations, the development of an effective and scalable model of implementing lifestyle intervention in real-world settings has the potential to benefit millions of people at risk of diabetes and other noncommunicable diseases.

In conclusion, this large trial in screen-detected individuals at increased risk of diabetes, building on the foundation of Daqing Diabetes Prevention Study, is expected to generate critical insights for public health professionals. By evaluating the effectiveness of lifestyle interventions in a real-world setting, the study aims to inform strategies for optimizing resource allocation and enhancing intervention delivery for individuals with prediabetes. Ultimately, the findings could contribute to efforts to curb the rising epidemic of diabetes and other noncommunicable diseases.

sec.title: Trial status
sec.p: The first recruitment started in April 2024. Recruitment will be completed in October 2024. The current protocol is version 4 (dated November 20, 2025). The submission of this study protocol has been delayed due to the need to finalize key methodological aspects based on real-world implementation insights. Given the complexity of conducting a large-scale cluster-randomized trial in a workplace setting, additional time was required to ensure the feasibility of the screening process, optimize recruitment strategies, and refine intervention delivery based on initial participant engagement. Furthermore, aligning the study protocol with practical implementation considerations—such as digital intervention integration, adherence monitoring, and resource allocation—necessitated careful planning and coordination among stakeholders. This delay was essential to enhance the scientific rigor, feasibility, and long-term impact of the trial, ensuring that the protocol accurately reflects the study’s real-world application and sustainability.
